title: Building Your Architecture Practice
objectives: Establish and grow an architecture practice within your organisation
Define standards, patterns, and governance appropriate to your context
Build the business case for architecture investment
Connect your practice to cross-government communities
Measure the value your architecture practice delivers
whyThisMatters:
An architecture practice is more than having architects in the building. It is the combination of people, processes, and artefacts that together ensure an organisation makes coherent, informed technology decisions. Without a functioning practice, architecture becomes ad hoc — dependent on whichever architect happens to be in the room, producing inconsistent outputs, and unable to demonstrate its value to the organisation.

Many government departments either have no formal architecture practice (architecture happens informally through senior developers or is absent entirely) or have a practice that has lost credibility (seen as bureaucratic gatekeepers disconnected from delivery). Both situations produce the same outcome: poor technology decisions, duplicated effort, accumulating technical debt, and services that do not interoperate.

The Blueprint for Modern Digital Government and the RESET framework both emphasise building digital capability within departments. The DDaT Capability Framework defines architecture roles at multiple levels — from Associate to Principal — with clear skill expectations at each. But having people in DDaT architect roles is not the same as having a functioning practice. The practice is the ecosystem that enables those individuals to be effective: shared standards, reusable patterns, governance processes, knowledge management, and community connections.

Building a practice — especially from scratch — requires architectural thinking applied to the practice itself. You need to understand your stakeholders, assess your current state, design a target state, and deliver incrementally. This lesson applies everything you have learned about architecture to the meta-problem of establishing the practice that does architecture.

content.heading: What an Architecture Practice Actually Is
content.body:
An architecture practice comprises three interconnected elements: people, process, and artefacts.

People: the architects themselves — their skills, experience, career development, and community. A healthy practice has architects at multiple levels (Associate, Senior, Lead, Principal in DDaT terminology) with clear progression paths. It invests in developing its people through mentoring, training, community participation, and stretch assignments. It recruits deliberately to fill capability gaps rather than simply hiring whoever applies.

Process: how architecture work gets done — governance processes, review cadences, decision-making protocols, and engagement models with delivery teams. A healthy practice has clear processes that delivery teams understand and engage with willingly. It defines when architecture engagement is needed (discovery, alpha, beta, live), what form it takes (embedded architect, periodic review, design authority input), and how decisions are escalated and recorded.

Artefacts: the outputs the practice produces and maintains — architecture principles, patterns, reference architectures, technology standards, ADR repositories, technology radar, current-state landscape documentation, and target-state roadmaps. A healthy practice maintains living artefacts that teams actually reference and use, rather than shelfware produced for governance compliance and never read again.

The three elements reinforce each other. Good people produce good artefacts. Good processes ensure artefacts stay current. Good artefacts make processes efficient. Weakness in any element undermines the others — brilliant architects are ineffective without good processes, and excellent processes cannot compensate for missing capability.

Maturity levels of architecture practices:

Level 1 — Ad Hoc: architecture happens informally. No documented standards, no shared patterns, no governance. Individual architects may be excellent, but their work does not compound or persist.

Level 2 — Emerging: some standards exist. An ADR repository is started. Occasional architecture reviews happen. But architecture engagement is inconsistent and reactive.

Level 3 — Defined: clear governance processes, documented standards and patterns, regular architecture reviews, and defined engagement model with delivery teams. The practice is recognised as a function.

Level 4 — Managed: the practice measures its outcomes, continuously improves its processes, and demonstrates value quantitatively. Architecture decisions are data-informed. The practice influences strategy.

Level 5 — Optimising: the practice drives strategic technology decisions, contributes to cross-government architecture communities, publishes thought leadership, and is seen as a competitive advantage for the organisation.

content.heading: Building From Scratch vs Inheriting a Practice
content.body:
Building a practice from scratch is different from inheriting and improving one. Both are common in government — departments reorganise, new functions are created through machinery of government changes, and new CTOs arrive wanting to establish capability that did not previously exist.

Building from scratch:

Start with quick wins that demonstrate value. Do not begin by writing a 50-page architecture principles document that nobody reads. Instead: run your first architecture review on an active programme and catch a significant risk, create your first ADR template and help a team document a decision they were going to make anyway, or produce a current-state landscape diagram that makes visible something nobody had articulated before.

Establish your engagement model early. Delivery teams need to know: when should they involve architecture? What can they expect from the engagement? How long will it take? An engagement model that says 'involve us at discovery and alpha, we will provide a supporting architect embedded in your team' is more compelling than 'submit your designs to the review board and wait 3 weeks for feedback.'

Build relationships before building governance. Governance imposed by a new practice without established trust will be resisted. Spend the first 3-6 months being useful — helping teams, sharing expertise, resolving problems — before introducing formal processes. Teams that have experienced value from architecture will welcome light governance; teams that have only experienced delay will resist it.

Inheriting a practice:

Assess honestly before changing. The practice exists for reasons — understand what works before dismantling it. Talk to delivery teams (the practice's customers) not just to the architects. Ask: what value does the practice provide? What frustrates you? What do you wish it did differently?

Identify the quick reputation wins. If the practice has a reputation problem ('the department of no'), identify one or two visible changes that signal a new approach. Perhaps: reduce the ARB submission document from 30 pages to 5. Or change the governance model from 'approval required before you proceed' to 'advice available when you need it, mandatory review only at key milestones.'

Retain institutional knowledge while improving processes. The existing architects know the estate, the history, the stakeholders, and the political landscape. Changing processes should not mean replacing people. Involve existing team members in designing improvements — they know where the bodies are buried.

content.heading: DDaT Roles and Career Paths in Architecture
content.body:
The Digital, Data and Technology (DDaT) Capability Framework defines architecture roles at four levels in the UK Civil Service:

Associate Architect: typically 2-5 years of technical experience, working within a delivery team under guidance from a more senior architect. Focuses on detailed design within an established architecture. Learning the craft of architecture — how to document decisions, evaluate trade-offs, and communicate with non-technical stakeholders.

Senior Architect (also called Solution Architect): 5-10 years of experience, responsible for the architecture of one or more services. Makes significant design decisions, defines solution architecture for programmes, and engages with stakeholders up to service owner level. This is the most common architect role in government delivery.

Lead Architect: responsible for architecture across a portfolio of services or a significant domain (data architecture, integration architecture, security architecture). Defines standards and patterns for others to follow. Mentors Senior Architects. Engages with director-level stakeholders and contributes to departmental technology strategy.

Principal Architect (also called Chief Architect or Head of Architecture): sets the architecture direction for a department or major function. Defines the target-state enterprise architecture. Represents the department in cross-government architecture communities. Engages with CTO, CDO, and board-level stakeholders. Responsible for the architecture practice itself.

Career development in architecture is not purely about technical depth — it is about expanding your sphere of influence, stakeholder engagement level, and strategic thinking capability. The DDaT framework maps skills against each level, including: technical breadth, strategic thinking, communication, leadership, and understanding of government context.

A healthy practice provides clear progression: what does an Associate need to demonstrate to become a Senior? What opportunities exist for Lead and Principal progression? How does the practice support development through mentoring, stretch assignments, and community engagement?

Common career path challenges in government: the 'glass ceiling' where Senior Architects cannot progress because Lead/Principal roles are not established or funded; the 'isolation problem' where a department has one architect with nobody to learn from or benchmark against; and the 'delivery trap' where architects are so embedded in delivery they never develop the strategic capabilities needed for senior roles.

content.heading: Connecting to Cross-Government Communities
content.body:
No departmental architecture practice should operate in isolation. Cross-government communities provide: shared learning (what worked and failed elsewhere), shared patterns (why reinvent what HMRC already solved?), collective influence (architecture concerns raised by 10 departments carry more weight than one), and career development (exposure to different contexts and scales).

Key cross-government architecture communities:

The GDS Enterprise Architecture team (within OCTO — Office of the Chief Technology Officer): provides strategic direction for cross-government architecture, maintains cross-government patterns and standards, and coordinates architecture decisions that affect multiple departments. They convene architects across government and provide guidance on shared platforms and interoperability.

The Technical Design Council (TDC): brings together Chief Technology Officers from across the public sector to make strategic technology decisions. Architecture practices should ensure their department's CTO is briefed with architecture perspective before TDC discussions.

The cross-government architecture community: a community of practice where architects from different departments share experiences, discuss challenges, and develop shared approaches. Regular meetups (virtual and in-person), Slack channels, and collaborative working on shared problems.

The Technology Code of Practice (TCoP) community: focuses on how departments implement TCoP principles, sharing practical approaches to common challenges like legacy modernisation, cloud adoption, and open standards.

Domain-specific communities: security architecture community, data architecture community, integration architecture community — each focused on cross-cutting concerns that benefit from cross-government coordination.

How to connect effectively: contribute, do not just consume. Share your department's experiences — both successes and failures. Propose patterns that others might reuse. Offer to peer-review other departments' architectures. Present at community events about what you have learned. The departments that contribute most get the most back — because others want to help those who help them.

Practical steps: identify which communities exist (GDS maintains a directory), nominate representatives from your practice to attend regularly (not ad hoc), feed community insights back to your team, and actively share your work (publish ADRs, open-source reusable components, blog about your approach on Technology in Government).

content.heading: Measuring Practice Value and Making the Investment Case
content.body:
Architecture practices that cannot demonstrate their value get cut when budgets tighten. 'We prevented bad decisions' is true but hard to prove — you cannot easily demonstrate the cost of disasters that did not happen. Effective practices find ways to measure and communicate their contribution.

Quantitative measures:

Delivery velocity impact: do programmes with architecture engagement deliver faster than those without? Track time-to-live for services with and without architecture involvement. If architecture engagement adds 2 weeks of design time but saves 3 months of rework, that is measurable value.

Reuse metrics: how many teams reuse patterns, components, or platforms that the practice established? If 5 teams use the shared integration platform rather than building their own, quantify the saving (development cost × 5 minus the shared platform cost).

Technical debt metrics: is the rate of technical debt accumulation decreasing? Are legacy systems being modernised according to the roadmap? Track the percentage of services on supported technology stacks versus end-of-life platforms.

Incident reduction: do services with architecture reviews experience fewer critical incidents? Track incident frequency and severity for services that went through architecture governance versus those that did not.

Qualitative measures:

Stakeholder satisfaction: do delivery teams find architecture engagement valuable? Regular surveys (kept short — 5 questions maximum) provide trend data. If satisfaction is low, understand why and fix it before measuring again.

Strategic influence: is the practice consulted on strategic decisions? Are architecture recommendations implemented? Track how often the CTO or programme boards seek architecture input and how often recommendations are accepted.

Making the investment case:

The business case for architecture investment rests on: risk reduction (architecture governance catches problems before they become expensive), efficiency (shared patterns and platforms eliminate duplication), speed (clear standards reduce decision time and rework), and strategic alignment (architecture ensures technology investments support organisational goals).

Frame the case in language your audience understands. For finance colleagues: 'Architecture governance prevented £2M in duplicate platform spend this year.' For delivery leaders: 'Teams using our patterns deliver 30% faster in alpha because they are not making decisions from scratch.' For the CTO: 'Our technology roadmap reduced legacy risk from 14 end-of-life systems to 6 in 18 months.'

The counter-case — what happens without architecture investment: reference real examples from NAO reports on failed government programmes where architecture failures were cited. The Common Agricultural Policy delivery programme, the NHS National Programme for IT, and numerous others failed partly because of poor architecture decisions made without adequate architecture capability.

workedExample.title: Establishing an Architecture Practice in a Department Without One
workedExample.context: A mid-sized government department (3,000 staff, £200M annual budget, 15 digital services) has no formal architecture practice. Technology decisions are made ad hoc by senior developers and programme managers. There is no technology standards document, no ADR repository, no architecture governance, and no documented current-state landscape. The department recently failed a GovAssure assessment partly because nobody could articulate the technology estate or its interdependencies. The new CTO has hired a Lead Architect (you) with a mandate to establish an architecture practice. Budget: 1 Lead Architect (you) + 2 Senior Architect posts to recruit, plus a small amount for tooling.
workedExample.approach:
The Lead Architect treats establishing the practice as an architecture problem — assess current state, design target state, deliver incrementally.

Month 1-2: Discovery and Quick Wins
- Interview 10 delivery teams to understand: what technology decisions are they making? What do they wish they had help with? What would they value from an architecture function?
- Interview CTO, DDG, and programme directors to understand: what technology problems keep them awake at night? What visibility do they lack?
- Produce a draft current-state landscape diagram (even if incomplete) — immediately valuable because nothing like it existed before
- Help one live team with an urgent architecture decision — demonstrate value through action, not through documents about governance

Month 3-4: Foundations
- Publish v1 technology standards (intentionally brief — 2 pages covering: approved cloud platforms, programming languages, data stores, and integration patterns). Not exhaustive, just enough to stop the most common divergence
- Create an ADR template and repository. Seed it with 5 ADRs documenting decisions already made (retrospective ADRs for recent projects)
- Recruit first Senior Architect, focusing on delivery-embedded architecture to demonstrate immediate team-level value
- Establish fortnightly architecture community of practice (invite interested developers and tech leads — not just architects)

Month 5-6: Engagement Model
- Define when delivery teams should engage architecture: at discovery (optional — come if you want advice), at alpha (recommended — architecture review of proposed approach), at beta assessment preparation (required — validate operational readiness)
- Run first lightweight architecture reviews — 1-hour sessions, minimal paperwork, focused on helping rather than judging
- Recruit second Senior Architect, focusing on enterprise architecture to maintain the landscape and standards

Month 7-9: Governance and Measurement
- Establish a monthly Design Authority meeting — lightweight, focused on cross-cutting decisions and pattern sharing rather than approval/rejection
- Begin measuring: teams engaged, reviews conducted, patterns created, reuse instances
- Produce first quarterly report to CTO: 'here is what we did, here is the value, here is what we plan next'
- Connect to cross-government architecture community — attend meetings, share early experiences

Month 10-12: Maturity
- Technology Radar v1 published — showing the department's assess/trial/adopt/hold classifications
- Architecture principles documented (derived from experience, not imposed top-down)
- First cross-government contribution: publish a reusable pattern or case study
- Formal practice review: what worked, what did not, what next?
workedExample.outcome: After 12 months: 3 architects providing coverage across the portfolio, a functioning Design Authority that delivery teams attend voluntarily, documented standards that reduced technology fragmentation (new services choosing from 3 approved stacks rather than 12 different approaches), and a current-state landscape that the CTO references in board meetings. The department passes its next GovAssure assessment with specific praise for improved architecture visibility. Two delivery teams report that architecture engagement saved them 'months of rework' by catching integration issues early in alpha.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The critical success factor was starting with value delivery rather than governance. The first 6 months focused entirely on being useful — helping teams, producing artefacts people actually wanted, and building trust. Governance was introduced only after the practice had demonstrated its value and teams actively wanted the coherence it provides. The departments that fail at practice building typically do it the other way round: impose governance before earning trust, then wonder why teams resist.

civilServiceScenario.title: Justifying Architecture Investment When the CTO Questions Whether Architects Add Value
civilServiceScenario.background: You are the Lead Architect in a department with a small architecture practice (yourself and 2 Senior Architects). The department has a new CTO who came from a startup background. In their first month, they question the architecture function: 'In my experience, good developers make good architecture decisions. Why do we need dedicated architects? That is three senior salaries that could fund six developers who actually build things.' The CTO is not hostile — they genuinely want to understand the value. They have asked you to present a business case for maintaining (or expanding) the architecture practice at the next leadership team meeting in 2 weeks.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: Build a compelling business case that demonstrates the value of architecture investment in a government context, using evidence and examples that resonate with a delivery-focused CTO.
constraints: The CTO values speed of delivery above all — any argument must connect to delivery outcomes
The department has 15 live services and 5 in active development
Last year, two services had significant rework (3+ months each) due to architecture issues discovered late
The department spends £3M annually on a legacy integration platform that newer services work around rather than use
Three services independently built authentication systems before GOV.UK One Login was available — none can now migrate easily
The architecture practice is 18 months old and has documented 40 ADRs, published technology standards, and run 25 architecture reviews
Developer satisfaction surveys show that teams who engaged with architecture rated their delivery confidence 30% higher
You have 15 minutes to present, including questions
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Lead Architect building and presenting the business case.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
The CTO's challenge is legitimate and common — especially from leaders with startup backgrounds where dedicated architects are rare. The response must not be defensive ('architecture is important because TOGAF says so') but evidence-based and delivery-focused.

The strongest arguments connect architecture to the CTO's priorities:

1. Cost avoidance: the 3 duplicate authentication systems cost approximately £500K each to build. An architect identifying GOV.UK One Login as the strategic direction early would have saved £1M+ and avoided the current migration problem. Architecture investment: £180K/year. Cost avoided in this single example: £1M+.

2. Delivery speed: the two services with 3+ months of rework had no architecture engagement. That is 6 developer-months wasted — equivalent to 3 architect salaries for a year. Architecture reviews that catch issues in week 2 rather than month 8 pay for themselves.

3. Strategic coherence: the £3M legacy platform exists because no architecture function guided technology choices. Services built their own integrations. An architecture practice prevents the next £3M legacy platform from forming by guiding consistent choices today.

4. Developer productivity: with published standards and patterns, developers spend less time deciding 'which database should I use?' and more time building features. The 30% delivery confidence improvement from engaged teams suggests real productivity gains.

The framing: architects do not replace good developers — they multiply their effectiveness by providing context, preventing duplication, and catching problems early when they are cheap to fix rather than late when they are expensive.

practiceArtefact.description: Write a concise business case (maximum 2 pages) for establishing or expanding an architecture practice in your department. Include: the problem statement (what happens without architecture investment), proposed investment (roles, tools, processes), expected benefits (quantified where possible), risks of not investing, and a 12-month delivery roadmap. Tailor it to a CTO audience who values delivery speed and cost efficiency.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Use concrete examples from your experience or from published NAO/PAC reports on failed government technology programmes. Quantify where possible — cost of rework, cost of duplication, cost of legacy. Frame architecture as an enabler of speed, not a constraint on it. Address the common objection that 'good developers do not need architects' honestly — acknowledging the grain of truth while explaining what architecture provides beyond what individual developers can.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**Business Case: Architecture Practice Investment**

**Problem Statement:**
Without dedicated architecture capability, our department experiences: duplicate solutions (3 services built independent authentication — estimated £1M wasted), late-stage rework (2 services required 3+ months rework in the past year due to integration issues not caught early), technology fragmentation (12 different technology stacks across 15 services, increasing maintenance cost and reducing developer mobility), and legacy accumulation (£3M/year spent on a platform that newer services work around). Total estimated annual cost of architecture absence: £4-5M.

**Proposed Investment:**
- 1 Lead Architect (existing) — strategic direction, governance, stakeholder engagement
- 2 Senior Architects (existing) — embedded delivery support, reviews, patterns
- 1 additional Senior Architect (new) — enterprise architecture, landscape management, standards
- Tooling: architecture repository and diagramming tools (£15K/year)
- Total annual investment: ~£350K (fully loaded costs for 4 architects + tooling)

**Expected Benefits (Year 1):**
- Prevent 2 instances of late-stage rework: saving ~6 developer-months (£150K)
- Prevent 1 instance of solution duplication: saving ~£300K
- Reduce technology fragmentation: consolidate from 12 stacks to 6, reducing maintenance overhead by ~£200K/year
- Begin legacy platform migration: reduce £3M annual spend by 20% (£600K) within 2 years through planned modernisation
- Delivery speed: 20% faster time through alpha for services engaging architecture (based on current data)

**ROI:** £350K investment against £650K+ in year-1 savings and avoidance. Payback within 7 months.

**Risk of Not Investing:**
- Continued duplication and fragmentation
- Growing legacy estate with increasing maintenance cost
- Failed service assessments due to poor architecture visibility
- GovAssure non-compliance (demonstrated in last assessment)
- Inability to meet TCoP and Service Standard requirements at scale

**12-Month Roadmap:**
- Q1: Recruit additional architect, complete landscape assessment, publish technology standards v2
- Q2: Establish lightweight governance, begin legacy migration planning, launch architecture community
- Q3: First legacy system decommissioned, pattern library established, cross-government community connected
- Q4: Measure and report outcomes, plan Year 2 based on evidence

reflectiveQuestions: If your architecture practice disappeared tomorrow, what would break first? What would nobody notice for months? The answers tell you where your practice adds the most and least value.
How do delivery teams in your organisation perceive the architecture function — as a helpful partner, a bureaucratic gatekeeper, or something they are unaware exists? What shaped that perception?
What is your architecture practice's 'elevator pitch'? If a new CTO asked 'what do you actually do and why should I fund it?' in 30 seconds, what would you say?
Are you connected to cross-government architecture communities? If not, what are you missing by working in isolation? If yes, what have you gained from those connections?
How do you develop the architects in your practice? Is there a clear progression path, or do architects plateau at Senior level with nowhere to grow?

knowledgeCheck.question: What are the three interconnected elements of an architecture practice?
options: Budget, tools, and office space
People, process, and artefacts
Governance, standards, and compliance
Architects, developers, and managers
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A functioning architecture practice comprises people (architects with skills, career paths, and community), process (governance, engagement models, decision protocols), and artefacts (standards, patterns, ADRs, reference architectures). Weakness in any element undermines the others.

knowledgeCheck.question: When building a new architecture practice, what should you do first?
options: Write comprehensive governance documentation and establish an Architecture Review Board
Demonstrate value by helping delivery teams with immediate problems, building trust before introducing governance
Create a 12-month roadmap and present it to the board for approval
Hire a full team of architects before engaging with any delivery teams
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Trust must precede governance. A new practice that starts by imposing governance on teams that have not yet experienced its value will face resistance. Starting with practical help — assisting teams, producing useful artefacts, catching problems early — builds the credibility and relationships that make governance welcome rather than resented.

knowledgeCheck.question: How should an architecture practice measure its value?
options: Count the number of documents produced and meetings held
Combine quantitative measures (delivery speed, rework reduction, reuse metrics) with qualitative measures (stakeholder satisfaction, strategic influence)
Only measure cost savings from prevented failures
Architecture value cannot be measured and should not be attempted
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Effective measurement combines quantitative evidence (delivery velocity impact, reuse instances, technical debt reduction, incident rates) with qualitative feedback (team satisfaction, strategic influence). Neither alone tells the full story — quantitative measures miss intangible value while qualitative measures alone are not compelling to finance-minded stakeholders.

knowledgeCheck.question: What role does the GDS Enterprise Architecture team play in relation to departmental practices?
options: They replace the need for departmental architecture by providing all architecture centrally
They provide strategic direction, cross-government patterns, and coordination while departments own their local architecture
They audit departmental architecture practices and issue compliance ratings
They have no relationship with departmental architecture practices
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The GDS Enterprise Architecture team within OCTO provides strategic direction, maintains cross-government standards, and coordinates architecture decisions that span departments. Departmental practices own their local architecture while aligning with cross-government direction. The RESET framework reinforces that departments are accountable for their own architecture with central support rather than central control.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the strongest business case argument for architecture investment?
options: Architecture is required by TOGAF methodology
Evidence-based demonstration that architecture engagement reduces rework, prevents duplication, and accelerates delivery — quantified in financial terms
Other departments have architects so we should too
The Service Standard mandates a specific number of architects per service
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The most compelling business case uses evidence: quantified cost of rework prevented, savings from reuse enabled, delivery speed improvements measured in teams with versus without architecture engagement, and cost avoidance from prevented duplication. Abstract arguments about 'good practice' or 'compliance' are less persuasive to delivery-focused leadership than concrete financial evidence.
